# How The Hindu Turned My Sunday Filter Coffee into Toxic Waste

### A Mylapore man’s struggle against Ethical Non-Monogamy, Communist capitalism, and the Cockroach Janata Party

[](https://substack.com/@amaruvi)

A Mylapore Sunday rests on three pillars.

One: a mami shouting at the milkman because he came at 5:47 instead of 5:45.

Two: a degree coffee so perfectly frothed it deserves its own ISRO launch window.

Three: the soft rustle of *The Hindu* Sunday Magazine.

In the 80s and 90s, this third pillar was sacred. You opened the paper and found R.K. Narayan, Gangadhar, Art Buchwald — writers who understood that a Sunday supplement must accompany breakfast, not conduct a moral strip-search of the reader.

You read. You smiled. You folded the paper. You ate idli. You adjusted your veshti and continued with life. This was my life in Neyveli in the 80s and 90s.

Yesterday, in Mylapore, however, *The Hindu* did not accompany my breakfast.

It mugged it.

By 7:15 a.m., my idlis tasted like thermocol, my blood pressure had crossed the Bay of Bengal, and my filter coffee had the emotional aftertaste of Cooum water.

I had gathered some past issues of The Hindu Sunday magazine section. Plus the edition of 5th June, 2026

## First came Ethical Non-Monogamy

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

I opened the magazine expecting a piece on temple tanks, old Madras bungalows, or one retired violin vidwan in West Mambalam preserving varnams and acidity.

Instead I was hit by a 3,000-word article on **Ethical Non-Monogamy**.

Only our English-speaking elite can take one ordinary, middle-class sin, put it through a vocabulary washing machine, and relaunch it as a lifestyle framework and even be happy about it.

Adultery, apparently, is no longer enough. It must now be *ethical*. This means Google Calendar invites, Excel sheets of emotional boundaries, quarterly review meetings, and perhaps a shared Notion board titled *Intimacy Roadmap Q3*.

My wife looked over her glasses and asked, “What is ENM?”

I should have pretended to faint. Instead, like a fool who enjoys danger, I explained.

“It means,” I said, “that if I go to Nalli Silks, I may also take the neighbour mami to inspect Kanchipuram sarees, provided you have signed an MoU regarding my emotional bandwidth.”

She looked confused.

“A is married to B while C is married to D. But A goes out with D while B goes with C. And this arrangement is known to A,B,C and D,” I said and lowered my eyes.

The look she gave me could have stripped paint off a Pallavan bus.

Twenty eight years of marriage, two LIC policies, one SBI locker, and a stable household ceasefire — all endangered because *The Hindu* decided Mylapore households need relationship anarchy before breakfast.

## Then came Communist capitalism

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

I turned the page hoping for relief.

Instead I found a Communist leader explaining free-market capitalism.

Pause and admire the achievement. A lifelong Marxist was offering the nation advice on venture capital, liquidity, and ease of doing business. This is like asking a strict Iyengar mama to host a masterclass titled **“101 Exciting Egg Recipes for the Modern Home.”** ( Have you hear of a person by name D.Raja anywhere in the media in the last 3 years ? You can see him in The Hindu when Prachanda or Baby, unknown to outside words, vacate their place in the paper’s real estate.

Apparently the market must remain free, but under the moral supervision of people who still speak of the Soviet Union as if Brezhnev has stepped out only for coffee and will return after one Gold Flake.

And *The Hindu*, naturally, gave this the solemn treatment usually reserved for constitutional amendments, monsoon failures, or M.S. Subbulakshmi anniversaries.

## Then came the DMK halo service

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every paper has political leanings. Fine.

But *The Hindu’s* relationship with the DMK has now moved beyond editorial sympathy and entered temple-kumbabhishekam sponsorship territory.

In a normal newspaper, if a flyover cracks, a road caves in, or a contract goes to somebody’s cousin’s driver’s brother-in-law, the reporter asks questions.

In *The Hindu*, every scandal arrives pre-washed, perfumed, and wrapped in ideological tissue paper.

If a drain overflows, it is not bad governance. It is the hydrological expression of social justice.

If a road disappears after one drizzle, it is not corruption. It is a challenge to Brahminical asphalt.

If a tender goes to a politically adjacent relative, it is not nepotism. It is inclusive redistribution with family values.

Ancient alchemists tried to turn copper into gold. *The Hindu* has gone one better and turned municipal incompetence into moral virtue.

Icing on the cake was the then head of The Hindu, N.Ram, taking the avatar of a photographer for M.K.Stalin when the latter was the Chief Minister.

Now that Stalin has been asked to take rest and a new Chief Minister is in place, the paper is still figuring out how to do a balancing act so as not the jeopardise the government advertisements while at the same time appear to be sticking to the erstwhile liaison with the DMK lest the party conducts the upanayanam to the paper and rechristens it as ‘Mount Road Mahavishnu’.

## Then came the literary trauma buffet

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Just when I thought the morning had peaked, the paper served up a reverential article about Umar Khalid’s prison reading habits.

I have no objection to prison reading habits. Let everyone read. But why should I know what are the books that the secessionist in jail had read and his views on those books ? An entire page for that ? This was preceded by a couple of editorials in the past weeks on the need to grant bail to the terrorist sympathiser.

And then came the review like interview of Meena Kandasamy’s latest book.

Friends, there are cyclones, there are tax notices, and then there are *The Hindu* reviews of the likes of Meena Kandasamy.

This was not a review. It was a public flogging delivered in postmodern English. Every paragraph arrived armed with words like **hegemony**, **subversion**, **embodied rage**, **structural violence** and many other terms that seemed to declare that I was the accused.

After three paragraphs I was no longer a reader. I was the convict.

I began to feel guilty for my veshti, my coffee filter, my scooter, and possibly the entire Chola empire.

After I read the piece, I went to lock the front door of my apartment lest some policeman should barge in and arrest me for all my wrong doings, as per Meena’s interview.

In my youth, a book review made you want to buy a book.

Today it makes you want to call a lawyer.

## Then, inevitably, came the Cockroach Janata Party

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

No Sunday supplement is complete without *The Hindu* dragging in the **Cockroach Janata Party** — that indestructible political organism that has been brought into life by some unseen force that no one wants to talk about. The daily ridicule of normal intelligence that happens at Jantar Mantar in the name of democracy is given a decent coverage - a visit by the usual suspects Brinda Karat et al and all other protest-hungry-souls who have nothing to do as the only communist government in Kerala has also been retired recently.

This CJP party has one great talent: it loses ground in the real world and gains column inches in *The Hindu* at the exact same time. It isn’t even a party yet.

It is the political equivalent of that one cockroach in the kitchen which survives Hit spray, Good Knight, phenyl, chappal attack, and three generations of family hatred.

And yet the paper treats this motley crowd like a council of philosopher-kings.

At the moment, the same travelling circus is camped at Jantar Mantar, where the protest has already acquired the full Delhi ecosystem: hunger strike, solidarity selfies, opposition cameos, microphones, tote bags, and the general mood of a college culturals committee accidentally merging with an India Habitat Centre panel discussion.

Let four and a half spokesmen gather in a studio and say something vague about secularism, federalism or the soul of India, and immediately they are granted the gravitas once reserved for freedom fighters, Finance Ministers, or at least people who have won a ward election without losing their deposit.

If five retired uncles at my nephew’s upanayanam stand near the bajji counter and discuss geopolitics, nobody gives them a 1,200-word think piece.

But let the same level of confusion emerge from the Cockroach Janata Party, and *The Hindu* treats it as a profound democratic intervention.

## The real problem

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The real problem is not even the politics.

It is the mood.

Everything in the Sunday supplement now feels like a lecture delivered by a disappointed postgraduate who wants me to feel morally compromised before my second tumbler of coffee.

Every article wants to deconstruct me, unsettle me, educate me, or make me apologise for a thousand years of structural wrongdoing before I have even finished my chutney.

Where is the wit? Where is the lightness? Where is the old newspaper pleasure of a beautifully written column about one eccentric uncle in Srirangam who still keeps pickle accounts in a 1974 ledger and thinks UPI is a CIA plot?

If R.K. Narayan submitted a Malgudi column today, I am convinced some assistant editor would reject it with the note: **“Charming, but insufficiently attentive to caste capital, domestic patriarchy and postcolonial spatial anxiety caused by dialectical materialism.”**

## The verdict

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

I want my old Sunday paper back.

I want essays, wit, railway nostalgia, temple tank trivia, and one harmless profile of an 83-year-old violin repairer in Mylapore.

I do **not** want relationship anarchy, Communist capitalism, literary trauma, Cockroach Janata Party analysis, and moral guilt sermons before breakfast.

I had been forced to take the most drastic step available to a Mylapore male of a certain age.

I had cancelled my subscription thrice, with the same Service Request Number SR-1775573. But still continue to get the paper but not the refund cheque. Must be one of the wonders of coffin stage communism that the paper espouses.

Henceforth, my coffee would be accompanied by R.K.Narayan’s ‘Bachelor of Arts’ or ‘The Financial Expert’. That way, I could at least be saved from the weekly dose of book reviews on queer literature and progressive approach to take another man’s wife out in the name of ENM just to appear progressive.

What is your tale ? Say in the comments.
